On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Udayaditya is the active, commanding force and Sitaram the helpless subordinate. The Yubaraj, sword in hand, kicks open the locked door, draws his weapon, and demands passage; Sitaram, bound by the Maharaj's orders yet unwilling to fight the man who saved his life twice, can only ask to be disarmed, surrender his weapon, and be tied head to foot so he will have an excuse before Pratapaditya. Udayaditya binds him with his own cloth and leaves him lying there — the prince literally immobilizes the guard while he engineers the escape.

On the night of the prison escape, every element of that relationship inverts. Sitaram is now the free, decisive agent: he is secretly orchestrating events (whispering news to Basanta Ray and hurrying him out of the palace), and when the fire breaks out he throws open the prison door, tells Udayaditya to come out, and grabs him, almost carrying him to safety. Udayaditya, by contrast, has been reduced to passivity by long confinement — standing in the open field, he can only ask helplessly, "What should I do? Where should I go?" It is Sitaram who commands, "Come, come with me!"

The reversal also settles a debt. Sitaram had refused to bear arms against Udayaditya because the prince saved his life twice; on the second night he repays that mercy by becoming the rescuer himself. The man who was once bound on Udayaditya's orders now physically seizes and liberates him — savior and saved, binder and bound, exchange places completely.

Pratapaditya's first attempt: he secretly hired two Pathans to murder Basanta Ray on the road to Jessore, at the inn in Simultali. The plot failed because the assigned Pathan, won over by the old king's kindness and delight in his music (and having already earned enough "merit," preferring worldly gain), could not bring himself to do the deed. His brother lured Basanta Ray's retainers away on the pretext of a dacoit attack, but the killer instead confessed the whole conspiracy to Udayaditya and sought Basanta Ray's protection.

What finally succeeded: after Udayaditya was lured out and captured in a field near Raigarh, Muktiyar Khan entered the fort in plain clothes with soldiers, presented Basanta Ray with a death sentence written and signed in Pratapaditya's own hand, and after the old king forgave him, embraced him, and entrusted Udayaditya to his care, Muktiyar had his subordinate Abdul behead the praying king with a sword.

1. **The inner quarters (Mahishi's room) of the Jessore palace, disguised as a middle-aged woman ("Mother Nikasha")** — after he had taunted the palace ladies and the Mahishi, Rammohan gripped his hands, hoisted him into the air, then bound him in a shawl and carried him out over his shoulder like a sack.

2. **Ramchandra Ray's palace chamber in Chandradwip, undisguised as the king's jester** — when he crudely mocked Vibha (the princess of Jessore) as she begged the king, Rammohan grabbed him by the scruff of the neck and threw him out of the room.

Rukmini—the widow known as "Mangala"—covertly prepares a poison (disguised as a tantric medicine, requested secretly by the Rajmahishi through Matangini to win back the Yubaraj's heart) and works spells so Udayaditya feels no pity. Surma takes this poison and dies by her own hand, so it is this secret poisoning—not the exile decree—that actually removes her from the palace.

By refusing to leave with Rammohan, Vibha deeply insulted Ramchandra Ray. To avenge his wounded honor, the king married another woman. When Vibha finally arrives in Chandradwip, Rammohan tearfully informs her that the Maharaj is getting married that very day—there is no place for her in her own kingdom or the royal palace. Having reached the very gates of the palace, all her hopes of happiness vanish "like a mirage": she faints from the shock, learns he offers no forgiveness, and—dressed as a common beggar-woman—insists on going to see him once more, her world utterly shattered.

Rukmini extracts the ring from Udayaditya when she confronts him at night during a storm; unable to bear her sitting on Surma's bed, he offers her anything she wants, and she demands the ring from his finger.

Sitaram, who is deep in debt to Rukmini and scheming with her, recruits Bhagavat to plot against the Yubaraj. They write a forged petition designed to look as though Udayaditya is lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor in order to seize the kingdom for himself. Because Rukmini's ring bears a seal engraved with the Yubaraj's name, they stamp the fake petition with it, making it appear authentically sealed by Udayaditya.

Bhagavat then carries the petition not to Delhi but to Pratapaditya, claiming a servant of Udayaditya had been fleeing toward Delhi with it and that he intercepted it. Though the king privately doubts the Yubaraj would do such a thing, the sealed "evidence" gives him his pretext: he orders Udayaditya imprisoned, guarded so he cannot act in secret, while rationalizing that no hardship will come to him.

The escape itself did not summon any decree against Surma; its consequences rippled until they reached her. Because Udayaditya broke out of the inner quarters that night by overpowering the guards, Sitaram (and Bhagavat) were dismissed from service. Sitaram sank into poverty with a household of dependents, and Udayaditya, feeling responsible, fixed a monthly stipend for the two dismissed men. News of this reached Pratapaditya, who—now paying special, jealous attention to Udayaditya—was enraged that his son was honoring the men he had punished, and he forbade any further help. Udayaditya would not abandon the starving families, so Surma took the burden on herself, secretly sending the stipends through a trusted maid. When word of that secret aid reached Pratapaditya, he said nothing but ordered Surma sent to her paternal home—the exile decree that finally forced her out.

**Emotional significance:** The song is a lament of desolation and survival — the grief of outliving everyone one loved. Its lines ("What was there has gone away; what remains is only emptiness... Those who were once mine no longer answer my call") express the emptiness of old age when joy remains but the people to share it with are gone. The broken sitar that "can no longer be tuned" mirrors this: the music of his life has fallen permanently out of tune.

**The two contrasting contexts:**

1. **In Raigarh (private, anticipatory loneliness):** Sitting alone on his veranda at sunset, Basanta Ray hums the song to himself as a spontaneous, half-philosophical meditation. It stems from vague longing — memories of festive visits to Jessore — and yet the scene still holds warmth: Khan Saheb arrives, comforts him, and soon the old man is swept up singing the lively "Tajbe Taj Naube Nau," clapping and joyful. The sorrow here is tempered, distant, almost aesthetic.

2. **In Jessore (shared, realized grief):** After learning of Udayaditya's imprisonment, he finds the once-joyful palace dark and silent. Standing before the desolate room that used to burst into celebration at his arrival, hearing Vibha confirm "no one at all" is left, he takes her hand and slowly sings the same line aloud. Now the song is no longer reverie but a dirge — the feared loss has become real, and what he once sang alone he now shares with the sole broken remnant of the household, uniting their grief.

In short, the same song moves from private nostalgia amid continuing companionship to public lament over an actual, confirmed ruin.

At the canal, Rukmini fails to stop Udayaditya — the boatmen pull her off Sitaram, her curse goes unheeded, and the boat casts off with the escapee. Rather than dying, she survives her leap into the floodwaters and returns burning for revenge.

Her failure converts directly into denunciation: barging into Pratapaditya's court, she exposes the entire conspiracy — that Sitaram orchestrated the fire, and that the old king of Raigarh conspired to steal the Yubaraj away. The men sent with her return confirming Udayaditya is in Raigarh, and she remains there, later pinpointing the Yubaraj in the evening field for Muktiyar Khan's soldiers.

Armed with this intelligence, Pratapaditya issues his secret orders to Muktiyar Khan. When the soldiers capture Udayaditya outside Raigarh, a second, sealed order is revealed: a death sentence for Basanta Ray, punishment for harboring the fugitive. Udayaditya's desperate pleas — offering himself as a prisoner, challenging the army to battle, crying out a warning — all fail against Muktiyar's insistence that there is no sin in obeying the master's orders.

Thus the chain runs: Rukmini's failed interception → her survival and vindictive testimony → Pratapaditya learning the truth of the escape and its architect → the execution order → Abdul's bloodied sword in Basanta Ray's prayer room. Had she succeeded at the canal, there would have been no escape to expose, no Raigarh conspiracy to punish, and no death sentence for the old king to carry out.

In Chapter 8, Pratapaditya asserts his superiority through cold, understated indifference: no music or lights to welcome the son-in-law, only a late escort of the Dewanji with a modest retinue and a small elephant, and at the audience itself no joy or haste — a calm "Come. Are you well?", attention given to a minister's documents instead of his guest, an interruption when Ramchandra tries to speak about the floods, and a curt dismissal to the inner quarters. His dominance needs no display; Ramchandra leaves quietly recognizing "in what way Pratapaditya was superior to him."

In his own court later, Ramchandra inverts this dynamic through manufactured, theatrical superiority. hypersensitive to honor, he tries and terrorizes a poor man merely for discussing the Pratapaditya–Ramchandra comparison, then presides over daily sessions where courtiers empty "verbal arrows" into Pratapaditya's back: the Dewan claims Pratapaditya's father had to weep and plead before Ramchandra's grandfather for anointment with the little toe of his left foot, and Ramai Bhand derides his lineage — grandfather an earthworm, father a leech bloated on his subjects' blood. Ramchandra laughs, savors his hookah, and lacks the nerve to stop any of it.

The contrast is pointed: Pratapaditya's authority is effortless and real, conveyed through a few indifferent words, while Ramchandra's is compensatory and second-hand — built on flatterers' ridicule, forced punishments, and rewritten genealogies — revealing a small, vain man still smarting from that original humiliation.

Rukmini, the widow who ensnared him in his youth at Raigarh, later left there, renamed herself Mangala, and settled on the outskirts of Jessore. Ambitious to rule both the Yubaraj's heart and the kingdom, she befriended all the palace servants, kept track of every scrap of palace news, and even performed tantric rites praying for the deaths of Pratapaditya and Surma. When the King and the Rajmahishi's hostility toward Surma finally led to a proposal to send her from the palace, the Rajmahishi—hoping to win back the Yubaraj's heart before dismissing Surma—sent Matangini to fetch medicine from the widow, knowing her skill in tantra, mantra, and medicine. Mangala spent five days grinding roots and chanting mantras to prepare not a love-potion but a poison, ritualistically ensuring the Yubaraj would feel no pity when Surma died. Surma, on the eve of her departure, took the poison and died at dawn in Udayaditya's lap. Thus the widow of his youthful shame re-entered his life and destroyed its one source of happiness. Afterwards, exploiting his grief, she even stole into his darkened bedchamber one stormy night as he mourned, playing the wronged woman, demanding his love, and extorting his ring—all part of her scheme to ensnare him once more.

In the opening chapter, Udayaditya's complaint is already a wish for renunciation in embryo: he laments that in a royal family one is born only as an heir, never as a son, and he openly wishes he could undo his birthright, asking what penance could reverse being crown prince. He even declares that he would abandon everything and flee with Surma—only her presence holds him back. His failure at the Hosenkhali pargana, his father's contempt, and the court's verdict that he is unfit to rule have convinced him that the throne is a burden he can never carry.

By the final chapter, catastrophe has destroyed the tie that kept him: brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he freely confesses what he has believed all his life—"I am not worthy"—and asks not for mercy but for release from the succession. The old private lament is thus consummated as a public, irrevocable act: swearing before Ma-Kali that he will never accept even a needle's tip of the kingdom, naming Samaraditya heir, and begging only to be released rather than caged. The wish he once voiced at a window at night becomes a formal oath in the temple, and its fulfillment takes the shape he himself had imagined—exchange the palace for the lowliest station, ending as an ascetic at Kashi establishing a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle's name. What began as helpless complaint ends as chosen renunciation: the penance he asked for in Chapter 1 is finally granted by his own oath in Chapter 34.

Ramchandra Ray, stung in his pride and urged on by advisers, writes a rash letter to Pratapaditya declaring that he has renounced Vibha and that she must never be sent to Chandradwip again. The elderly Nayanchand, who is entrusted with carrying it, is terrified of what Pratapaditya might do if he reads it, so instead of delivering it to the king he privately hands it to the Mahishi.

The Mahishi, already overwhelmed with grief over Vibha and the imprisoned Udayaditya, dare not show it to Pratapaditya—fearing catastrophe—nor tell Vibha, fearing the delicate girl would not survive the news. When Basanta Ray visits Jessore, she confides the letter to him. After reading it, he advises her to show it to no one, to send Vibha to her father-in-law's house at once regardless of honor, and—crucially—to proclaim in the household that Ramchandra has written *requesting* that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip.

Thus the letter's true, spiteful message is inverted: Vibha is told her husband has summoned her out of love. She is overjoyed, believes he understood and forgave her, and eagerly begs her mother to send her soon—while the mother, concealing her own dread, delays and weeps behind her smiles.

Pratapaditya's trap had two parts, and both failed. First, he ordered the canal adjoining the palace—where Ramchandra's boat lay—blocked with large sal wood logs, and posted guards so no one could leave the inner quarters. But the geography itself betrayed him: the palace roof towered only about seventy cubits above that same canal, so Rammohan simply twisted thick sheets into a rope, tied it to a rooftop pillar, and lowered Ramchandra straight down into his sixty-four-oared boat, bypassing every locked door and guard.

Second, when the blocked canal stopped the boat, Rammohan and his men hauled it up and over the logs. The guards' pursuit then collapsed in farce: they had swords but no guns, and by the time a flintlock was found there was no gunpowder or bullets; the man sent for a chase boat stopped to smoke a pipe of tobacco at Harimudi's shop and detoured to wake Ramashankar over a debt, so the boat arrived long after it was needed—while the scolding that followed took three times longer than the delay itself.

The boat slipped away to the Bhairav river, where Fernandez fired a cannon—startling Pratapaditya awake to find his own guards had fled.

Basanta Ray's sitar mirrors his inner state throughout. It is first presented as his "eternal companion," the natural outlet for everything he feels—when words fail him at parting, he picks it up and plays furiously, trying to drown out Vibha's tears and his own. But even the sitar cannot hold back his grief: his eyes blur, his throat chokes, and he has to set it down.

His deepest gesture comes at the moment of leaving Udayaditya: "I am leaving this sitar behind, Dada, I will not play it anymore." Abandoning the instrument is a symbolic renunciation of joy itself—since the person he made music for is being taken from him, the music has lost its meaning.

By the time he sits alone in Raigarh, the sitar is gone from his side, and his explanation is telling: "It's not that I don't have the sitar. The sitar is there, only its strings have broken, and it can no longer be tuned." The broken strings are his broken heart—damaged by separation from Udayaditya and beyond repair. Just as the sitar cannot be tuned, his spirit cannot be restored to its old harmony.

Yet feeling is not dead in him, only displaced: he still hums sad songs ("I alone am left behind") and can be briefly swept up in Khan Saheb's singing. The outburst of music is a momentary attempt to revive his old self. It collapses the instant Sitaram arrives with news of Udayaditya's imprisonment—Basanta Ray stops singing abruptly, cannot absorb the news, and ends not with music but with a broken cry: "Dada, come to me! No one understood you."

In this way the sitar's arc—from constant companion, to abandoned at parting, to an instrument with broken strings—tracks his despair precisely: each stage of separation from Udayaditya silences his music further, until the imprisonment news takes from him even the pretense of song.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for his courage and readiness to involve himself in the affairs of the subjects, acting against even the king's wishes—he would treat danger as a trifle and fight oppression with all his might, stopping abusive officials without considering the consequences and protecting victims outright. After Surma's death, a blind, superstitious fear of Pratapaditya paralyzed him: when he heard of a plan to loot and burn the Chhapra zamindar's office, he had his horse readied but then abandoned the intervention; when a tied subject being beaten cried for mercy, he could not bear the sight but simply fled indoors instead of rescuing him; and when the stipends of Bhagavat and Sitaram were stopped, he repeatedly resolved to send money but hesitated each time and never did, whether openly or secretly. Notably, this was not fear for his life—he had no greater attachment to life than before—but a mysterious terror in which he saw his entire fate as clenched in Pratapaditya's fist, so that even at death's door a frown from his father could summon him back.

By conspiring with Bhagavat, Sitaram helped forge the treasonous petition bearing the Yubaraj's seal, which was delivered to Pratapaditya and led directly to Udayaditya's imprisonment. He ultimately undoes this by staging a fire near the prison: as the guards abandon their posts to deal with the blaze, Sitaram throws open the door of Udayaditya's cell, urges him out, and physically escorts him out of the prison to freedom—liberating the very man his forged petition had put behind bars.

On the first occasion, after Udayaditya forces open the locked doors of the inner quarters, Rammohan flees with Ramchandra Ray via the palace roof: he twists thick sheets into a huge rope, ties it to a pillar above the canal where the sixty-four-oared boat waits, climbs down with Ramchandra clinging to his back, then—at the rope's end—grips it with his teeth, frees Ramchandra, and lowers him by hand into the boat before jumping down himself; when the canal is found blocked with sal logs, he and his men haul the boat up and over them.

On the second occasion, after the king coldly disowns the humiliated Vibha and she faints, Rammohan—having thrown the mocking jester Ramai Bhand out of the room—renounces his hereditary service, lifts the unconscious Vibha in his arms, carries her out of the palace, places her in a palanquin by the gate, and takes her back to the boat (and onward to Kashi).

In both extractions he relies on his own colossal strength—back, arms, and teeth—moving a helpless royal to a waiting boat by sheer physical power.

In Jessore, Vibha was adorned as a royal bride—against her own taste. The Mahishi loaded each of her arms with eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet (when Vibha wanted thin turquoise ones), forced a large nose ring onto her small face, and styled her hair to her own insistence, even undoing the hairstyle Surma had secretly done to Vibha's liking. Vibha carried this heavy coiffure, nose ring, and armfuls of bangles as a "burden," flustered but glowing with joy.

In Chandradwip, stripped of all that grandeur, she deliberately dressed as a common woman—like a beggar-woman—refusing even a palanquin, insisting on going as an ordinary subject. She walked through the crowd veiled, entered the palace like a maidservant with no one to welcome her, and was so plainly clad that the king himself mistook her for a beggar woman seeking alms.

The shift is radical: from a princess weighed down by imposed, magnificent ornamentation marking her royal status, to a woman who voluntarily sheds every mark of rank, presenting herself as destitute and anonymous—her outer plainness mirroring her inner desolation.

In the bedchamber, the window is a frame of memory and absence. Udayaditya drifts to it because it was Surma's place—he sits there while leaving her spot empty—and what it shows him is a world hauntingly unchanged: the same moonlight, the same garden, the same breeze. Its symbolism is the cruelty of continuity; the view is identical to what it was when Surma sat there, and that very sameness makes her absence unbearable, feeding his fantasy that she has only stepped away and might still appear on such an evening. The window looks backward, at a happiness that is irretrievably lost.

In the prison cell, the window's meaning is inverted. It is now a tiny slit offering only a sliver of sky, a bamboo grove, and a temple, yet it becomes a promise of liberation: watching birds through it, he is convinced his cage will one day break and he too will swim in the boundless sky. He tells Vibha that on the small patch of floor before it he is "naturally free," beyond the reach of any king or emperor, while the soft bed across the room is his true prison. Here the window looks forward—it is hope, futurity, and the indestructible freedom of the inner self.

The change is thus from window-as-wound to window-as-release. In the palace, a free man at an open window feels imprisoned by grief, since the unchanged view only measures what can never return; in the cell, a captive at a barred slit feels free, since even a fragment of sky restores the future. In both scenes he sits sleepless at the window, but the first is a vigil for the dead and the second a vigil for a freedom still to come.

Their relationship collapses in three stages, each reversing the terms of the one before.

It begins as a comic inversion of a love affair: Sitaram, penniless but vain, courts Rukmini's silver as much as her beauty, borrowing money he never intends to repay and covering the debt with theatrical endearments—"Pran," "Priye," "Priyatame"—which she playfully extracts, and which he instantly spoils by joking about interest. She tolerates him because lending to him keeps a line into the palace; he stays because her cash and affection cost him nothing but flattery. Their "great secrecy" is conspiratorial intimacy: two schemers using each other, each confident they are the manipulator.

The arrangement breaks the moment their interests collide. Both actually orbit Udayaditya—Rukmini as a rejected mistress who still considers him *her* Yubaraj ("Only I can do him good, and only I can harm him"), Sitaram as his devoted, if absurd, champion. When Udayaditya is imprisoned, Sitaram turns on Rukmini with curses and threats of fire and public humiliation. Her fury is not really at the insults but at the claim of ownership: Sitaram presumes to be the Yubaraj's sole protector. What had been flirtation becomes rivalry over the same man.

The final encounter strips away all comedy. Sitaram, having burned the prison to free Udayaditya, assumes Rukmini is dead, plans to loot her money—"if I don't take it, someone else will"—and walks in on a phantom: a drenched, ash-faced, half-mad woman who has "returned from the door of Yama." The old script of feigned tenderness briefly resurfaces—Sitaram tries honeyed words, even "shall I sing that song?"—but now every endearment enrages her further. The woman who once demanded love-words wants only to lay him and the Yubaraj "in the oven" and smear herself with their pyre-ash; she reaches for a curved blade and hacks at the floor where he stood. He flees Jessore that night, and she completes the betrayal by exposing the entire escape plot to Pratapaditya.

In short: a loan sustained by mutual pretense of love curdles once both reveal that their true attachment is to Udayaditya. Flirtation gives way to threats, threats to attempted murder and mutual destruction—each discovering that the other was never the partner, only the obstacle.

Sitaram's plan works in escalating stages, each one building on the last:

**Stage 1 — The distraction.** The fire begins in the guardhouse huts near the prison, where the guards kept all their belongings. Because Udayaditya sat so passively in his cell that no one believed he would ever try to escape, the guards at his door were the first to abandon their posts to save their possessions. With the way cleared, Sitaram enters the cell and physically hauls Udayaditya out under the pretext that the prison itself is burning, spiriting him by boat across the canal to the river and to Basanta Ray.

**Stage 2 — Sustaining the chaos.** This was no ordinary fire that simply had to burn itself out. Sitaram's planted men infiltrated the firefighting effort itself: pouring water where there was no fire, fetching water and never returning, "accidentally" breaking their pots, and stumbling into one another. Spectators drawn by the spectacle further hampered real efforts. The result is a prolonged, self-renewing emergency that keeps every guard occupied and away from the prison.

**Stage 3 — Controlling the evidence.** Even before the physical cover-up, Sitaram sanitizes the record: he retrieves Udayaditya's letters from his messenger, keeps only the harmless ones addressed to the Mahishi and Vibha, and destroys the rest. He also takes the Yubaraj's sword when leaving the boat — a deliberate acquisition, as its next use shows.

**Stage 4 — Destroying the scene and manufacturing a death.** With the cell empty, Sitaram's men set fire to it directly — windows, doors, beams, rafters, fences. Since no one could conceive of a fire starting in the prison, nobody attends to it until it has taken hold. Sitaram then throws bones, a skull, and the sword into the blaze, fabricating the physical remains of a corpse.

**Stage 5 — Seeding the testimony.** Sitaram himself orchestrates the "witnesses": a man reports the Yubaraj's cell is aflame, another claims to have heard the Yubaraj screaming from inside, and Sitaram himself arrives shouting that the roof has collapsed and there is no response. Before the court later assembles, one witness swears he saw the Yubaraj at the window, others heard screams, and the melted remains of the sword are produced — exactly the fabricated proof needed.

In short, the fire evolves from a mere diversionary alarm into a self-perpetuating emergency, then into the destruction of the crime scene, and finally into a staged death complete with planted remains and rehearsed testimony — designed, as Sitaram himself reflects, to let him "remain untroubled for some time" while the trail went cold. The single flaw in the cover-up is Mangala (Rukmini), who survives his assumptions of her death, knows everything, and ultimately exposes the entire conspiracy to Pratapaditya — forcing Sitaram to flee Jessore entirely.

In his court, Ramchandra treats Udayaditya not as a savior but as a target of ridicule. When Ramai Bhand jokes that Udayaditya landed in trouble for thwarting the plan, Ramchandra laughs along, and the courtiers tear both Udayaditya and Pratapaditya to shreds with verbal arrows. His ingratitude stems from several beliefs: he assumed that if he was in peril, everyone would naturally unite to save him—so the rescue was owed, not a favor; he convinced himself Udayaditya acted only for his own sister's sake, not to save Ramchandra's life; and he lacked the mental courage to stop the mockery, worrying about what everyone would think of him. Being a fickle, small-minded man who weighed himself heavier than the whole world on the flatterers' scales, he simply joined the jeering at his brother-in-law.

Initially, Pratapaditya treats the Emperor of Delhi with open contempt—declaring "the Emperor of Delhi is not my God," ridiculing those like Mansingh, Birbal and Basanta Ray who tremble at his anger, and silencing his minister whenever the Emperor's name is raised. Yet the minister's warnings already cast the Emperor as a live danger: a complaint has been lodged against Pratapaditya in Delhi, and Pratapaditya himself suspects his own son Udayaditya of having done it.

That latent fear is later weaponized against him. When the king's unjust decision ruins Sitaram's and Bhagavat's livelihoods, the two conspire to topple him by striking at this exact weakness: they forge a petition as if the Yubaraj (Udayaditya) were accusing his father of treason before the Emperor of Delhi in order to seize the kingdom for himself. It is stamped with the Yubaraj's own seal—the ring Rukmini had brought—so the forgery carries his name. Bhagavat then carries the petition not to Delhi but straight to Pratapaditya, claiming a servant of Udayaditya was fleeing toward Delhi with it and that he intercepted it.

Because Pratapaditya had already voiced suspicion of his son and had declared himself "the judge of the Emperor of Delhi," the forged document convinces him that Udayaditya has betrayed him by allying with the very power he scorned. The imperial authority he publicly dismissed as irrelevant thus becomes, through a fabricated act of appeal to it, the evidence of treason by which his son is imprisoned. The threat he refused to fear in the open destroys his house from within, through a lie written in his son's name.

Vibha's hair traces Surma's arc from beloved companion to mourned absence. On the festive day of the son-in-law's visit, when the Mahishi imposes her own old-fashioned taste—thick gold bangles, a heavy nose ring—Vibha endures it all silently, except in one act of quiet defiance: she slips away to Surma to have her hair done to her own liking. That styling is the single gesture of intimacy and autonomy in an otherwise suffocating adornment, marking Surma as the one person in the Jessore palace who understands and serves Vibha's own heart.

After Surma is gone, the same daily ritual becomes a vigil of absence. When it is time to braid her hair, Vibha sits quietly "as if Surma will come at any moment to braid it for her"—but evening falls, night approaches, and her hair remains unbraided. The unattended hair is the precise negative image of Surma's presence: the hands that once braided it no longer come, and no one else takes their place.

Later, the neglect deepens into visible desolation—Rammohan, arriving after long silence, sees at once that her hair is unkempt, proof that "there is no one here to care for you." Thus the hair moves from styled (Surma's living presence), to unbraided (waiting and disbelief), to unkempt (abandonment and grief), serving as an outward barometer of Vibha's inner loss.
